title: A Trading Post at Singapore
arc: In January 1819, Raffles seeks a British trading post on Singapore, but the Temenggong who governs the island cannot grant land on his own. The student helps navigate a preliminary agreement, then a disputed succession as Raffles decides whether to sign a treaty.

documents.title: Reconstructed account of Raffles's instructions
documents.body: Raffles was told to establish a post at the southern end of the Straits, but to avoid a collision with the Dutch. Those two parts of his task must be considered together. Finding a useful place is not enough if the way it is obtained leads to a dispute. A first conversation with the people who govern the place may show whether a post is possible. Before any promise is written down, the visitors should ask what permission can be given now and what must wait for another person. A hurried answer may seem helpful today but leave the meaning of an agreement unclear tomorrow.

documents.title: Unsigned draft urging a quick agreement
documents.body: Sir, the visitors wish to know whether they may begin a trading post. A clear answer today would let everyone speak of the same plan instead of carrying different messages between the shore and your compound. Set down a first agreement now; leave the question of who may grant land for another day. The paper could say what the visitors hope to do first, while other questions are discussed later. Waiting to settle every question before writing anything may make even a small beginning difficult. This draft offers a quick course, though it does not say whose permission a grant of land would require.

glossary.meaning: a version that is not yet final

documents.title: Reconstructed list of treaty payments
documents.body: Terms to check before any treaty is signed. The Company would be permitted to establish a trading post at Singapore. The Sultan would receive 5,000 Spanish dollars each year, and the Temenggong would receive 3,000 Spanish dollars each year. These are yearly payments, not a single payment made on the day of signing. Check that the two amounts are kept separate when the terms are read aloud. This list records the proposed payments; it does not settle the question of which claimant should be recognised as Sultan.

glossary.meaning: a person who says a position or title is theirs

documents.title: Unsigned note proposing a limited harbour agreement
documents.body: A lasting treaty is not the only possible way to discuss a port. A short-term permission to use the harbour could let ships trade while the rival claim is sent to Calcutta for review. Such a permission would need a clear end date and words explaining what could happen before that date. The people asked to consent should hear those limits in plain language. There is no need to delay over further objections: a temporary arrangement should be simple to put into effect. This note offers a proposal, not a record that anyone has accepted it.

endings.title: The Treaty of 6 February
endings.summary: Raffles recognises Hussein as Sultan, and Raffles, Hussein and the Temenggong sign the treaty establishing a Company trading post. Farquhar becomes Resident and Commandant.

citations.quote: On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed between the East India Company, represented by Raffles, Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman.
Raffles appointed Farquhar as Resident and Commandant and sailed for Bencoolen on 7 February, having spent little more than a week on the island.

endings.epilogue: Your simulation: 6 February 1819. You see Raffles recognise Hussein as Sultan. Raffles, Hussein and the Temenggong sign a treaty allowing the Company to establish a trading post at Singapore. The Sultan is to receive 5,000 Spanish dollars a year and the Temenggong 3,000. Raffles appoints Farquhar Resident and Commandant, then sails for Bencoolen on 7 February. The Dutch protest, and for several years you cannot be sure whether Britain will keep the settlement. In 1824, the Dutch withdraw their objection under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty.

Seeking his permission might reduce the risk of a clash, but it does not secure a post. The Temenggong governs Singapore, yet only the Sultan can lawfully grant land to the Company. endings.title: A Limited Harbour
endings.summary: Raffles proposes time-limited port rights with Hussein's and the Temenggong's consent, rather than an immediate lasting treaty. He asks Calcutta to review the rival claim before proceeding further.
endings.epilogue: Your simulation: early February 1819. You help explain Raffles’ proposal to Hussein and the Temenggong: the Company may use the harbour for a limited time, while Calcutta reviews the rival claim to the throne. With their consent, ships could begin calling at Singapore, but this is not a lasting grant of land. The arrangement might give British traders the harbour they need without forcing an immediate decision about who can grant permanent rights. You also know why it may not settle the matter: the Dutch recognise Hussein’s younger brother as Sultan.

reveal.whatHappened:
Raffles wanted a British trading post near the route to China, but his instructions told him to avoid a clash with the Dutch. He arrived off Singapore on 28 January 1819 and landed near the Singapore River the next day. On 30 January, he and Temenggong Abdul Rahman signed a preliminary agreement for a trading post. The Temenggong governed the island, but only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company.

The throne was disputed. The Dutch recognised the younger son of the former Sultan, Abdul Rahman; Raffles considered the elder son, Hussein, to have the stronger claim. Hussein arrived in Singapore in early February, and Raffles recognised him as Sultan. On 6 February, Raffles, Hussein and the Temenggong signed a treaty allowing the Company to establish a trading post. Farquhar became Resident and Commandant. The Dutch protested, and it remained uncertain for several years whether Britain would keep the settlement.
interpretations: One reading puts trade first: Raffles was trying to secure a harbour for British merchants, and the choice of Singapore served that aim. His instructions, however, also warned him not to clash with the Dutch.

Another reading puts the disputed throne at the centre. Raffles considered Hussein's claim stronger because he was the elder son. The Dutch recognised Abdul Rahman instead and regarded him as the lawful ruler. Whether the treaty settled the question depended on whose claim was accepted.
corrections: The draft letter presses for a quick written agreement while setting aside who could grant land. The sources say the Temenggong could agree to a preliminary trading post, but only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company.

The harbour note makes a temporary arrangement sound simple and leaves out possible objections. The sources say the Johor throne was disputed, the Dutch protested against the British presence, and it remained uncertain for several years whether Britain would keep the settlement.
couldHaveGone: The Temenggong might have waited for a Sultan to take part because he governed Singapore but could not lawfully grant land to the Company himself.

A landing without a written agreement was plausible as a cautious first step: Raffles had landed near the river before the preliminary agreement was signed, and his instructions warned against a clash with the Dutch.
Raffles might have sought further instructions because Calcutta had warned him to avoid a clash with the Dutch, who recognised a different Sultan.

Approaching Abdul Rahman was another possible path because he had been installed as Sultan and the Dutch recognised him. It would, however, have meant dealing with the ruler whose claim Raffles did not consider the stronger one.
